strengths: Impressive systems achievement: the paper convincingly demonstrates, for the first time, real-time (20 FPS) streaming generation with a 14B-scale diffusion model, resolving the fidelity-vs-speed tradeoff that prior real-time approaches (CausVid, LongLive, Ditto) sidestepped by shrinking model size. This is a meaningful milestone for the field and fits an Applied/Systems contribution type, which is assessed on system-level impact rather than algorithmic novelty.

The Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a clean, well-motivated inference design that converts the sequential denoising chain into a spatial pipeline; the ablation (Table 3) clearly quantifies its impact (4.26 FPS without TPP vs. 20.88 FPS with it) and identifies VAE decoding as a separate bottleneck, which is honest and informative engineering analysis.

The Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (AAS + Rolling RoPE) and History Corrupt are well-justified against a clear diagnosis of long-horizon failure modes (inference-mode drift, distribution drift), supported by ablations (Table 4) and an unusually rigorous 10,000-second autoregressive stress test in the supplementary material showing stable metrics across sampled segments.

The supplementary finding that noise-aligned (same-timestep) KV caches outperform clean KV caches in both efficiency and perceptual quality is an interesting, useful insight for the streaming diffusion community, with a plausible explanation tied to pretraining conditions.

Evaluation is relatively thorough: quantitative comparisons, ablations, a double-blind user study, an additional in-domain AVSpeech evaluation with FID/FVD, detailed pseudocode for all training/inference algorithms, and clearly stated limitations (TTFF not improved by TPP, dependence on RSFM). LLM usage and ethical considerations are disclosed.
weaknesses: The main comparison benchmark (GenBench) is self-constructed by the authors using generated content (Gemini, Qwen-Image, CosyVoice), with no ground-truth video; FID/FVD are therefore excluded from the headline comparisons. Although the supplementary AVSpeech held-out evaluation partially mitigates this, the primary evidence base is a bespoke benchmark where the authors' data pipeline choices could favor their model. Publicly recognized avatar benchmarks would strengthen the case.

Numerical inconsistencies across tables undermine confidence in the reported results: Table 3 reports 'Ours' at 20.88 FPS with 5 GPUs, while Table 6 reports the same 20.88 FPS figure with 4 GPUs; the caption/text around 'w/ SP4GPU' (disabling multi-GPU parallelism vs. sequence parallelism of 4 GPUs) is confusing; Table 2 FPS values for baselines are identical across short and long video, suggesting they were copied rather than measured per setting. These need correction for reproducibility.

Algorithmic novelty is modest and heavily derivative of prior work: the training recipe follows Self-Forcing/CausVid (diffusion-forcing pretraining + DMD), and the sink-frame/rolling-cache ideas build on LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and Self-Forcing++. The contribution is best viewed as careful co-design and integration; individual components (TPP = timestep-sharded pipelining; AAS = sink replacement; Rolling RoPE = positional re-anchoring) are incremental refinements.

The TPP gains come at a nontrivial hardware cost (5 H800 GPUs plus a dedicated VAE GPU), and the reported TTFF of ~2.9s limits true interactivity, as the authors concede. A cost-normalized comparison (quality vs. GPU count) against baselines would make the deployment claims more transparent; Ditto at 21.8 FPS on a 0.2B model shows competitors remain far cheaper per stream.

User study is small (20 participants) and results are mixed relative to the narrative: WanS2V outscores the proposed method on Synchronization (85.2 vs. 80.6) and Consistency (92.0 vs. 91.1), so 'most balanced scores' is a favorable interpretation rather than a dominant result. The claim of state-of-the-art perceptual quality should be stated more cautiously.

Some important design details (exact History Corrupt noise magnitude/statistics, RoPE shift schedule, KV window ablations over length) are deferred or only qualitatively described, which limits reproducibility even with the provided pseudocode; no code or project page link is verifiable in the submission (project page field is empty).

strengths: The system-level achievement is significant: running a 14B diffusion model at ~20 FPS end-to-end for streaming avatar generation is a concrete and useful result, and the Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) idea of assigning one denoising timestep per GPU to turn the sequential diffusion chain into an asynchronous pipeline is a sensible engineering contribution.

The long-horizon consistency analysis (inference-mode drift vs. distribution drift) is reasonable, and the Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (AAS + Rolling RoPE) plus the 10,000-second stress test (supplementary Table 7) go beyond the few-minute horizons of prior work, with results that appear stable across segments.

The paper includes ablations for the main components (TPP, VAE parallelization, DMD, AAS, Rolling RoPE, History Corrupt), a double-blind user study, detailed runtime metrics, and full pseudocode in the supplementary material, which supports transparency.

The observation that noise-aligned (same-timestep) KV caches outperform clean KV caches both in efficiency and quality (supplementary Sec. 9.1) is an interesting and useful empirical finding for the streaming diffusion community.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: the framework is largely an assembly of existing techniques — Diffusion Forcing pretraining, Self-Forcing DMD distillation, rolling KV caches, attention sink mechanisms (LongLive, Rolling Forcing, StableAvatar), and pipeline parallelism are all established. The individual components (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE) are small modifications of these, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is genuinely new versus inherited.

The primary quantitative comparison is conducted on GenBench, a self-constructed benchmark generated with Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, and CosyVoice. Evaluating against baselines on synthetic prompts the authors themselves created, rather than established public benchmarks (e.g., standard talking-head test sets), weakens the credibility of the SOTA claims and makes results hard to compare across the literature.

Inconsistencies and gaps in evaluation: the main text promises FID/FVD evaluation but Table 2 omits them (they appear only in the supplementary AV-Speech table); the efficiency ablation (Table 3) compares configurations with different GPU counts (2 vs. 4 vs. 5), confounding FPS comparisons; some baseline FPS numbers (e.g., Ditto at 21.8 FPS on a 0.2B model) are reported under single-GPU conditions that may not be equivalent.

Fairness of the 'first to achieve real-time high-fidelity avatar generation at this scale' claim is questionable: Rolling Forcing and other concurrent works claim real-time streaming long-video generation, and the novelty rests mainly on the 14B model scale inherited from Wan-S2V rather than on the method itself.

Reproducibility is a concern: training consumed ~500 GPU days on H800s, the project page is blank in the submission, and no code/model release is confirmed. The synthetic GenBench test set construction is also not reproducible without release. For a paper whose main contribution is a deployment system, the lack of released artifacts substantially reduces its value to the community.

The 10,000-second extrapolation experiment repeats the same ~10-minute audio to fill the duration, which is a somewhat artificial stress condition; and the limitation section itself admits TPP improves FPS but not TTFF, and that dependence on RSFM may compromise long-term consistency — partly undercutting the headline claims.

Writing quality is uneven: several references are cited incorrectly (e.g., Self-Forcing cited with two different arXiv IDs, Wan-S2V duplicated under [14] and [15] with conflicting entries), Table 1's checkmark/cross formatting is inconsistent with the caption, and the main claims rely on qualitative evidence for some baselines' degradation.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important and previously unsolved problem: real-time streaming audio-driven avatar generation with a large (14B) diffusion model, and convincingly demonstrates the first such system at 20 FPS end-to-end on 5 H800 GPUs, which is a meaningful milestone over prior work that achieved real-time only with much smaller models.

The algorithm-system co-design is well motivated: Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a clean and novel reparameterization that converts the sequential diffusion chain into an asynchronous spatial pipeline, with low communication cost (latents only) and local KV reuse; the insight that same-noise-level KV caches both enable TPP and improve quality is interesting and validated (Table 6, supplementary).

The Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (AAS + Rolling RoPE + History Corrupt) directly addresses the two failure modes (distribution drift and inference-mode drift) behind long-horizon collapse, and the 10,000-second stress test (Table 7, Figure 9) with stable metrics across segments is strong evidence for the infinite-length claim.

Experimental evidence is fairly comprehensive: comparisons against six strong baselines on both OOD (GenBench) and in-domain (AVSpeech) sets, efficiency ablations decomposing FPS/TTFF gains (Table 3), component ablations (Table 4), a double-blind user study, and detailed pseudocode for all training/inference procedures, supporting reproducibility.

The paper is generally clearly written with good figures explaining the training pipeline, TPP schedule, and inference mechanisms; the limitations section honestly identifies that TPP does not reduce TTFF and that RSFM may compromise temporal consistency in complex scenarios.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evaluation is on a self-constructed benchmark (GenBench) generated by the authors using proprietary tools (Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, CosyVoice). While OOD evaluation is valuable, there is no evaluation on standard public talking-head benchmarks, which makes cross-paper comparison and verification of the claimed state-of-the-art difficult.

Several reported metrics are relatively weak or ambiguous: FID on AVSpeech (64.0) is notably worse than Ditto (46.3) and OmniAvatar (50.4); Sync-C on GenBench trails OmniAvatar substantially, and the justification relies on a single small user study (20 participants) without statistical analysis; ASE/IQA from Q-align are proxies whose correlation with human judgment is not established here.

The novelty is somewhat incremental when decomposed: the individual ingredients (Self-Forcing DMD distillation, diffusion-forcing pretraining, same-timestep KV caching, sink-frame/attention-sink ideas, rolling caches) are largely inherited from CausVid, Self-Forcing, LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and TalkingMachines; the contribution lies mainly in the combination, the TPP systems engineering, and the History Corrupt / AAS / Rolling RoPE refinements, and the paper could better delineate its delta over these very recent concurrent works (e.g., Rolling Forcing already proposes rolling-window denoising with attention sink).

TPP requires 5 H800 GPUs per stream, which is a heavy deployment footprint for 'practical' real-time generation; the paper does not discuss throughput-per-dollar comparisons or whether the same model could be served with fewer GPUs at reduced quality, nor memory costs of the per-timestep KV caches.

Some important details are deferred to the supplementary material (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE specifics), and the main text has minor inconsistencies (e.g., WanS2V cited as [14] and [15]; Table 7 labeled 'Ablation Study' though it reports long-horizon stability); the VAE decode offload to a 5th GPU means the headline FPS number is not from the 4 denoising GPUs alone.

The 10,000-second extrapolation evidence relies on metric tables over repeated 10-minute audio inputs; qualitative drift phenomena (subtle identity/color changes) may not be fully captured by ASE/IQA/DINO-s sampled at sparse intervals, so the 'no observable quality decay' claim could be substantiated with more rigorous drift measurements or released videos.

strengths: Strong and clearly demonstrated system result: the paper convincingly shows the first practical real-time (45 FPS, TTFF 1.21s) streaming generation with a 14B diffusion model, addressing both the real-time-fidelity trade-off and long-horizon drift.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a clean, well-motivated idea: assigning each GPU a fixed timestep converts the sequential denoising chain into an asynchronous pipeline, and the design naturally aligns with the timestep-forcing KV-cache strategy. The efficiency ablation (Table 3) carefully isolates the contribution of each component (DMD, SP4, TPP, VAE parallelization, kernel optimizations).

The three long-horizon strategies (History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE) are individually motivated by distinct failure modes (error accumulation, distribution drift, conditioning drift) and validated by targeted ablations (Table 4, Table 6), including a novel temporal-flicker metric comparison of KV-cache noise schedules.

Unusually thorough supplementary material: complete pseudocode for training and inference, 10,000-second extrapolation stress test (Table 7), in-domain AVSpeech evaluation with FID/FVD, a double-blind user study, block-size ablation, FP8 quantization analysis, and detailed kernel/system descriptions. The limitations section is honest and specific.

Introduction of GenBench (short/long) with videos exceeding five minutes addresses a real gap in standardized long-form avatar evaluation; the long-video comparison (Table 2) shows baselines degrade substantially while the proposed method remains stable.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on existing components: the two-stage causal adaptation is built directly on Self-Forcing/DMD and WanS2V. The novelty rests mainly on TPP, History Corrupt, AAS, and Rolling RoPE; individual pieces (attention sinks, RoPE repositioning, noisy caches) have precedents (e.g., StreamingLLM-style sinks, History-guided video diffusion), so the contribution is closer to well-executed combination and systems integration than fundamentally new modeling. This is acceptable for an applied/systems contribution, but the framing as multiple 'novel' mechanisms somewhat oversells.

Main quantitative comparisons (Table 2) are on the self-constructed GenBench only, and the benchmark/data will only be released in the camera-ready version, weakening reproducibility and external verification at review time. Baselines are run at 'official defaults' with heterogeneous parallelism (Ditto on a single GPU vs. the proposed method on 5 GPUs), so the headline FPS comparison is not fully like-for-like; the 70x-parameter FPS comparison mixes hardware configurations.

Quality metrics rely heavily on LLM-based evaluators (Q-Align ASE/IQA) and Sync metrics that the authors themselves note can diverge from human perception; claims such as 'surpassing the teacher on visual quality' are explained by DMD output-distribution concentration, i.e., plausibly metric artifacts. The user study (20 participants) partially mitigates but is small, and WanS2V still wins on naturalness there.

Key technical details (AAS, Rolling RoPE) are deferred entirely to the supplementary material, which reduces the readability of the main paper; the approach also depends on a static-scene prior (acknowledged as a limitation), constraining generality of the 'infinite-length' claim to avatar-like scenarios.
Training cost (128 H800 GPUs) is reported only sparsely; no wall-clock training cost analysis, which matters for assessing reproducibility and practical adoption of the distillation pipeline.

strengths: As an Applied/Systems contribution, the paper delivers a compelling end-to-end result: real-time (45 FPS, TTFF 1.21 s) streaming inference of a 14B diffusion model for audio-driven avatar generation, which appears to be genuinely beyond the current state of the art and is well-aligned with the declared contribution type.

TPP (Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism) is a clean and well-motivated systems idea: fixing one denoising timestep per GPU converts the sequential sampling chain into an asynchronous pipeline, and it composes naturally with the timestep-forcing KV-cache design rather than being an ad-hoc optimization.

Experimental evidence is unusually thorough for a systems paper: an incremental efficiency ablation (Table 3) decomposing FPS/TTFF gains, long-horizon stability ablations (Tables 4, 6), denoising-step and block-size studies, an FP8 quantization check (Table 11), a small user study (Table 9), an in-domain AVSpeech comparison with FID/FVD (Table 8), and a 10,000-second stress test with per-segment metrics (Table 7).

The diagnosis of long-horizon failure modes (test-time conditioning drift, distribution drift, error accumulation) is clearly articulated, and each proposed remedy (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE) is tied to a specific failure mode and validated in the ablations.

Reproducibility is supported by complete pseudocode for training and inference (Algorithms 1-4), detailed kernel-level optimization descriptions, runtime metric definitions, and a declared benchmark (GenBench) with release promised; limitations and ethical considerations are discussed candidly, including the ~3 s end-to-end latency and the static-scene prior.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is modest relative to the framing: the core components build directly on Diffusion Forcing, Self-Forcing, and DMD distillation. History Corrupt, AAS, and Rolling RoPE are sensible engineering fixes, and AAS in particular makes the 'generalizability' claim fragile, since replacing the user's reference image with the model's own first latent could systematically alter the subject's appearance at long horizons; the identity/quality metrics cannot fully detect this because Dino-S is computed against the reference image, not against generated content.

The 'infinite-length' claim is overstated. The 10,000-second stress test loops a ~7-minute audio clip and relies on a static-scene prior with a single persistent sink frame; stability is largely guaranteed by construction (identity anchored to one frame) rather than by genuine long-horizon modeling. Metrics evaluated on 10-second sampled segments cannot capture slow degradation modes such as gradual pose drift or background rigidity.

Comparison fairness is questionable: the headline 45.2 FPS uses 5×H800 GPUs plus heavy kernel optimization (FP8, FlashAttention-3, torch.compile, VAE caching), while Ditto reaches 21.8 FPS on a single GPU and other baselines are near or below 1 FPS partly due to limited parallelism support. A per-GPU-cost-normalized efficiency comparison is missing, and the claimed 70×-parameter advantage conflates architectural gains with system-level optimizations.

The primary benchmark (GenBench) is self-constructed, synthetic (generated with Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, CosyVoice), and not released at review time, so all headline comparisons rest on a non-public test set designed by the authors. The small AVSpeech held-out set (50 clips) and 20-participant user study provide limited statistical power; no variance or significance is reported anywhere.

Some quantitative wins are marginal or self-acknowledged: on Short videos Sync-C gains over OmniAvatar are small (7.03 vs 6.77) and Sync-D is slightly worse; ASE is below OmniAvatar and StableAvatar; the explanation that DMD distillation 'surpasses the teacher on visual quality' is given post hoc via an RL interpretation rather than demonstrated.

Clarity issues undermine polish: the running title is 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length', key details for two of the three claimed contributions (AAS, Rolling RoPE) are deferred to supplementary material, and heavy reliance on Table 3's 'Kernel Opt.' bundle obscures which optimization drives which FPS gain.

strengths: Strong, well-integrated algorithm-system contribution: the paper convincingly addresses both the real-time and long-horizon challenges for a 14B-scale diffusion model, achieving 45 FPS / 1.21 s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs and stable generation beyond 10,000 seconds—an unprecedented result in this space (Table 7, Fig. 7).

The technical ideas are well-motivated and complementary: History Corrupt (noisy KV cache as dynamics–identity decoupling), Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism each map to a clearly identified failure mode (error accumulation, distribution drift, conditioning drift, sequential bottleneck), and the ablations (Tables 4-6, Fig. 5) validate each component individually.

The empirical evidence is unusually thorough for this line of work: comparisons on two benchmark subsets (Table 2), an in-domain AVSpeech evaluation with FID/FVD (Table 8), a double-blind user study (Table 9), ablations over denoising steps, block size, KV-cache noise schedules, scaffolding convergence (Fig. 6), FP8 quantization (Table 11), and hardware-level pipeline timelines (Fig. 11).

The paper is transparent about limitations (static-scene prior, ~3 s end-to-end latency unsuitable for bidirectional interaction) and includes pseudocode, kernel-level implementation details, and an LLM usage statement that support reproducibility of the method.

Honest interpretation of results, e.g., acknowledging that Dino-S of Ditto is inflated by its face-editing nature, that WanS2V scores better on user-rated Naturalness, and that OmniAvatar's high Sync-C on long videos may be an artifact of visual collapse.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on prior art: the two-stage causal adaptation and DMD distillation closely follow Diffusion Forcing, CausVid, and Self-Forcing; the core novelty is more in the combination and engineering (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE, TPP) than in fundamentally new algorithms. Reviewers should assess this under an Applied/Systems lens, where the contribution is still substantial.

Reproducibility of the evaluation is currently weak: GenBench is self-constructed, synthetic (generated with Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, CosyVoice), and only promised for release 'in the camera-ready version.' The headline comparisons rest on this unreleased benchmark; releasing data and scripts should be a condition of acceptance.

Practicality concerns about the system claim: real-time performance requires 5 H800 GPUs with FP8 and extensive kernel optimizations; the cost profile relative to deploying a smaller real-time model (e.g., Ditto at 21.8 FPS on a single GPU) is not discussed beyond parameter count.

Minor internal inconsistencies and overclaiming risk: Fig. 1 states '20 FPS on 5 H800 with 4-step sampling' while the abstract and tables report 45 FPS; the 'first practical real-time streaming of a 14B diffusion model' claim depends on the precise definition of 'practical' and 'real-time.'

Some theoretical justifications are informal: the 'noise as low-pass filter' and 'noisy cache occupies a compact latent region' arguments (citing [36, 38]) are plausible but not substantiated quantitatively; the timestep-forcing benefit is largely empirical.

Metrics for long-horizon stability are mostly reference-free LLM-based scores (Q-Align) and per-segment DINO-S on self-generated audio; independent or standardized long-form metrics beyond the authors' own benchmark would strengthen the case. The user study (20 participants) is small.
